questions.question: What's the main problem with `public double Balance;` as a plain field?
options: Nothing stops external code from setting it to an invalid value like -1000
Fields can't be read from outside the class
questions.explanation: A public field has no way to run validation logic — any code can assign anything to it directly. Properties let you run code (like a range check) whenever the value is read or written.

questions.question: Given `public double Balance { get; private set; }`, which line fails to compile OUTSIDE the class?
questions.explanation: `private set` means only code inside the class itself can assign to the property. Reading (`get`) is still public. Assigning from outside the class is a compile error.

questions.question: What's the difference between `{ get; set; }` and `{ get; init; }`?
options: `init` can only be assigned during object construction (including an object initializer); `set` can be assigned any time
`init` is for value types, `set` is for reference types
`init` makes the property read-only forever, including during construction
questions.explanation: `init` allows assignment only during construction (e.g. `new Order { Id = "1" }`), then locks. `set` allows assignment at any point in the object's lifetime.

questions.question: You want to default to the simplest property that has no custom logic. Which do you write?
options: A full property with a private backing field
An auto-property: `public string Name { get; set; }`
questions.explanation: Auto-properties are the default choice — no extra ceremony, but still a property (not a field), so you can later add validation logic without breaking anyone who uses it.

questions.question: Which access modifier allows access from the SAME class only, not even from classes that inherit from it?
questions.explanation: `private` is the tightest — only code written inside that exact class. `protected` extends access to derived classes too (next lesson).

questions.question: Changing a public field to a property later, without changing its name or type, breaks code that uses `obj.Field = value;` or `Console.WriteLine(obj.Field);`.
questions.explanation: This is one of the reasons C# properties look like fields from the outside — `obj.Name = value;` and `Console.WriteLine(obj.Name);` work identically whether `Name` is a field or a property. You CAN swap a field for a property later without breaking callers — which is exactly why 'always use properties, even auto-properties, instead of public fields' is standard advice.
